1.note: Here Jeremiah wishes his head were **waters** and his eyes were **a fountain of tears**. He means that he wants to weep continually for his people. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I could produce tears without ceasing]

Jeremiah is referring to all of the time by naming two major components, **day** and **night**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [continually]

Jeremiah is using the adjective **slain** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [for the people who have been killed among]

Here Jeremiah is speaking of his fellow Israelites as if they were a **daughter**. He uses this expression to speak of his people tenderly, as a father would speak of his own child. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [my people, whom I love as my own child]

2.note: Jeremiah is using the question form to express a wish. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [I wish someone would give me a lodging place of travelers in the desert, that I might leave my people and walk away from them!]

Here Jeremiah is speaking of his people as if they were **adulterers**. He means that they have been unfaithful to Yahweh. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [For all of them are unfaithful to Yahweh]

Jeremiah is saying **all of them are adulterers** as a generalization for emphasis. If it would be clearer in your language, you could express the emphasis in a different way. Alternate translation: [almost all of them are adulterers]

3.note: Here Yahweh is speaking as if the people’s tongues were **their bow**, which they bend by treading on it in order to shoot lies. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And they prepare their tongues as weapons]

Yahweh is using **from evil thing to evil thing they go** as a common expression of the culture to mean “they commit one wicked act after another.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [For they proceed from one wicked act to another]

Jeremiah is using **the declaration of Yahweh** to indicate that what has been said is a direct quotation from Yahweh and comes with Yahweh’s authority. In your translation, use a natural way of indicating direct quotations in your language.

4.note: Yahweh is saying what he wants each person to do. See the discussion in the introduction to this book about the words “let” and “may,” and follow the decision of your team of how a speaker will express in this context what he wants someone to do. Alternate translation: [Each one of you must beware of your neighbor]

Here the masculine term **brother** has a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [do not trust any brother or sister]

Yahweh is repeating forms of the verb **deceives** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [every brother certainly deceives]

Here Yahweh is speaking of habitual behavior as if it were the way a person **walks**. He means that every neighbor regularly slanders others. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and every neighbor habitually slanders others]

5.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **iniquity**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [by doing what is wicked]

6.note: Here Yahweh is speaking as if deceit were a place where a person could live, since he says that Jeremiah’s **dwelling** is **in the midst of deceit**. He means that the people all around Jeremiah are constantly deceitful. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [You live among people who are constantly deceitful]
The pronoun **Your** refers to Jeremiah, whom Yahweh is addressing here. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [You, Jeremiah, dwell]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **deceit**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [among people who act deceitfully; because they are deceitful]

7.note: The word translated as **Therefore** indicates that what follows is a result of what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a result of what came before. Alternate translation: [As a result]

Here Yahweh is speaking of judging his people as if he were **refining** metal in a fire in order to remove what is impure from it. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Behold, I am purifying them and will test them]

Yahweh is using **Behold me** as an expression that people of this culture would commonly use to mean that they were about to do something. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Now I am about to refine them]

7.q: כִּֽי אֵ֣יךְ אֶעֱשֶׂ֔ה מִ⁠פְּנֵ֖י בַּת עַמִּֽ⁠י
7.note: Yahweh is using the question form to show that there is nothing else that he can do in response to what his people have become. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [for there is nothing else I can do in response to the daughter of my people.]

Yahweh is using **from before the face of** as a common expression of the culture to mean “because of the presentation of.” In this case, that “presentation” is of wickedness. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [because of the wickedness of]

8.note: Here Yahweh is speaking of what the people say as if their **tongue** were **a murderous arrow**. He means that their words destroy other people. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Their tongue destroys people]

Yahweh is not referring to a specific **neighbor**. He means such people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [With their mouths they speak peace toward their neighbors]
Here, **his mouth** represents what a person says. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [With his words]

Yahweh is using **he speaks peace** as a common expression of the culture to mean “he greets someone in a friendly way.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he greets his neighbor in a friendly way]

Yahweh is using **in his midst** as a common expression of the culture to mean “inwardly.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [but inwardly]

Here Yahweh is speaking of secretly planning to harm someone as if a person were setting an **ambush** for him. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he secretly plans to harm him]

9.q: הַ⁠עַל אֵ֥לֶּה לֹֽא אֶפְקָד בָּ֖⁠ם & אִ֚ם בְּ⁠ג֣וֹי אֲשֶׁר כָּ⁠זֶ֔ה לֹ֥א תִתְנַקֵּ֖ם נַפְשִֽׁ⁠י
9.note: Yahweh is using the question form to emphasize that he will certainly punish his people for what they have done. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [I will certainly punish them because of these things … I will certainly avenge myself on a nation such as this.]

By **visit upon them**, Yahweh means that he will punish them. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Shall I not punish them]

10.note: The pronoun **I** refers to Jeremiah. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [For the mountains I, Jeremiah, will take up weeping and wailing]

Jeremiah is using **take up weeping and wailing** as a common expression of the culture to mean “begin to mourn loudly.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will begin to mourn loudly]

Jeremiah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and for the pastures of the wilderness I will take up a lamentation]

The expression **they are burned up** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [because fire has burned them up]

Jeremiah is referring to all of the living creatures of the land by naming two major components, **the bird of the heavens** and **the beast**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [as for all the living creatures of the land]

The terms **fled** and **gone** mean similar things. Jeremiah is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [they have completely fled away]

11.note: At this point Yahweh begins to speak again, although the text does not introduce his words with a phrase such as “Yahweh says.” In your translation, use a natural way of indicating direct quotations in your language.

Here, **a dwelling-place of jackals** represents a place that people have abandoned. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [a place abandoned by people]

The term **jackals** describes a kind of wild dog that lives in deserted places. If your readers would not be familiar with what jackals are, you could use the name of a similar animal that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [wild dogs]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **a desolation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [desolate, so that no one lives in them]

12.q: מִֽי הָ⁠אִ֤ישׁ הֶֽ⁠חָכָם֙ וְ⁠יָבֵ֣ן אֶת זֹ֔את
12.note: Jeremiah is using the question form to emphasize that almost no one is wise enough to understand these things. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Hardly any man is wise enough to understand this.]

Here, **the mouth of Yahweh** represents Yahweh himself as the one who speaks. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Yahweh himself]

The point of this comparison is that just as **the wilderness** is dry and empty of people, so is the land after Yahweh judges it. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [burn up so that it becomes as dry and empty as the wilderness]

13.q: וַ⁠יֹּ֣אמֶר יְהוָ֔ה עַל עָזְבָ⁠ם֙ אֶת תּ֣וֹרָתִ֔⁠י אֲשֶׁ֥ר נָתַ֖תִּי לִ⁠פְנֵי⁠הֶ֑ם וְ⁠לֹא שָׁמְע֥וּ בְ⁠קוֹלִ֖⁠י וְ⁠לֹא הָ֥לְכוּ בָֽ⁠הּ
13.note: The word translated as **Because** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [And Yahweh said, “The land perishes because they have forsaken my law that I set before the face of them, and they do not listen to my voice, and they do not walk in it]

Here, **my voice** represents what Yahweh has commanded. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and they do not listen to what I have commanded]

Here Yahweh is speaking of obeying his law as if it were a path in which a person could **walk**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and they do not obey it]

14.q: וַ⁠יֵּ֣לְכ֔וּ אַחֲרֵ֖י שְׁרִר֣וּת לִבָּ֑⁠ם וְ⁠אַחֲרֵי֙ הַ⁠בְּעָלִ֔ים
14.note: Here Yahweh is speaking of following and serving something as if a person **walked after** it. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [But they have followed the stubbornness of their hearts and served the Baals]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **the stubbornness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what their stubborn hearts desired]

Yahweh is using the plural **the Baals** where he could have used the singular form. This suggests that he is using the plural form to refer to the many images of the god Baal that the people worshiped. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the singular and express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and after the many images of Baal]

15.q: לָ⁠כֵ֗ן כֹּֽה־אָמַ֞ר יְהוָ֤ה צְבָאוֹת֙ אֱלֹהֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל הִנְ⁠נִ֧י מַאֲכִילָ֛⁠ם
15.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [Therefore I, Yahweh of hosts, the God of Israel, tell you to behold, for I am feeding them]

Yahweh is using **Behold me, feeding them** as an expression of the culture to mean that he was about to do something. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Now I am about to feed them]

15.q: הִנְ⁠נִ֧י מַאֲכִילָ֛⁠ם אֶת הָ⁠עָ֥ם הַ⁠זֶּ֖ה לַֽעֲנָ֑ה וְ⁠הִשְׁקִיתִ֖י⁠ם מֵי רֹֽאשׁ
15.note: Here Yahweh is speaking of the suffering that he will bring on his people as if he were **feeding them** bitter **wormwood** and making them drink **water of poison**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Behold, I am bringing bitter suffering on them, this people, and causing them to endure deadly misery]

The term **wormwood** describes a kind of plant with a very bitter taste that people considered to be poisonous. If your readers would not be familiar with what wormwood is, you could use the name of a similar plant that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [bitter food]

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe **water** that is characterized by **poison**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [poisoned water]

16.note: Here, **the sword** represents warfare. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and I will pursue them with war]

17.note: The expression **the ones who chant laments** describes women whom people in this culture hired to sing mournful songs when someone had died. If your readers would not be familiar with such people, you could use the name of a similar kind of person that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [for the women who are paid to sing sad songs at funerals]

17.q: וְ⁠קִרְא֥וּ לַ⁠מְקוֹנְנ֖וֹת וּ⁠תְבוֹאֶ֑ינָה וְ⁠אֶל־הַ⁠חֲכָמ֥וֹת שִׁלְח֖וּ וְ⁠תָבֽוֹאנָה
17.note: These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [and summon the women who are skilled at chanting laments, so that they may come]

Yahweh is using the adjective **skilled** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [those women who are skilled at mourning]

18.note: Yahweh is saying what he wants the mourning women to do. See the discussion in the introduction to this book about “let” and “may” and follow the decision of your team of how a speaker will express in this context what he wants someone to do. Alternate translation: [They must hurry and wail for us, so that our eyes stream with tears, and our eyelids flow with water]

18.q: וְ⁠תֵרַ֤דְנָה עֵינֵ֨י⁠נוּ֙ דִּמְעָ֔ה וְ⁠עַפְעַפֵּ֖י⁠נוּ יִזְּלוּ מָֽיִם
18.note: Yahweh is using **our eyes may go down** and **our eyelids flow** as a common expression of the culture to mean “we will weep very much.” If these phrases do not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [that we may weep bitterly, and shed many tears]

18.q: וְ⁠תֵרַ֤דְנָה עֵינֵ֨י⁠נוּ֙ דִּמְעָ֔ה וְ⁠עַפְעַפֵּ֖י⁠נוּ יִזְּלוּ מָֽיִם
18.note: By **our**, Yahweh means the people of Judah but not the mourning women whom they are calling to come, so use the exclusive form of that word in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

19.note: The expression **is heard** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [people hear the sound of wailing from Zion]

Here, **Zion** represents the people who live in Jerusalem. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [from the inhabitants of Jerusalem]
If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [from Zion, that they are devastated]

The people of Jerusalem are using a phrase that expresses a strong feeling of grief and dismay. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [We are utterly devastated!]

The expression **we are devastated** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [our enemies have devastated us]
The pronoun **they** refers to the enemies who attacked Jerusalem. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [because our enemies have destroyed our dwellings]

20.note: Since Jeremiah is speaking to the **women** of Judah, the word **hear** and the word **your** are plural here. Use plural forms in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

Here, **your ear** represents your ability to listen, and **his mouth** represents what Yahweh says. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and use your ability to listen to receive the words he speaks]

Jeremiah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and let each woman teach her neighbor a lament]

21.note: Jeremiah is speaking of **death** as if it were a living thing that could climb up through windows and enter palaces. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [deadly disease has spread through our windows, it has spread into our palaces]

Here Jeremiah is speaking as if death would **cut off** the children and the young men from the places where they gather. He means that they will be killed. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to kill the children outside, the young men in the open plazas]

22.q: דַּבֵּ֗ר כֹּ֚ה נְאֻם יְהוָ֔ה וְ⁠נָֽפְלָה֙ נִבְלַ֣ת הָֽ⁠אָדָ֔ם
22.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [Speak this message from Yahweh, that the corpse of man will fall]

The point of this comparison is that just as **dung** lies scattered on a field and no one gathers it, so will the bodies of the dead lie on the ground with no one to bury them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and the corpse of man will lie unburied and disregarded like dung]

Yahweh is not referring to a specific **corpse**. He means the bodies of dead people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the dead bodies of people]

Yahweh is using **the face of the field** as a common expression of the culture to mean “the open ground.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [upon the open ground]

The point of this comparison is that just as **sheaves** lie on the ground behind a harvester when no one collects them, so will the bodies of the dead lie there with no one to bury them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and lying uncollected as cut grain lies behind a harvester]

23.note: Yahweh is saying what he does not want wise people to do. See the discussion in the introduction to this book about “let” and “may” and follow the decision of your team of how a speaker will express in this context what he wants someone to do. Alternate translation: [The wise one should not boast]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **wisdom**, **strength**, and **riches**, you could express the same ideas in another way. Alternate translation: [that he is wise … that he is strong … that he is rich]

24.note: Yahweh uses the word **But** here to indicate a contrast between the boasting that he forbids and the boasting that he approves. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Rather]

The terms **understanding** and **knowing** mean similar things. Yahweh is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [truly knowing me]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **covenant faithfulness**, **justice** and **righteousness**, you could express the same ideas in another way. Alternate translation: [what is faithful to my covenant, just, and right]

25.note: Yahweh is using the term **Behold** to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Listen carefully, days are coming]

Yahweh is using **days are coming** as a common expression of the culture to mean “there will be a time.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [a time is approaching]

The expression **being circumcised** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [all of the ones who have circumcised only their foreskin]

Yahweh is using **being circumcised in foreskin** as a common expression of the culture to mean “circumcised only in their bodies.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [all of the ones circumcised only in their bodies]

26.q: עַל מִצְרַ֣יִם וְ⁠עַל יְהוּדָ֗ה וְ⁠עַל אֱד֞וֹם וְ⁠עַל בְּנֵ֤י עַמּוֹן֙ וְ⁠עַל מוֹאָ֔ב
26.note: Here, **Egypt**, **Judah**, **Edom**, **Ammon**, and **Moab** represent “the people who live in those lands.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [upon the people of Egypt and upon the people of Judah, and upon the people of Edom and upon the people of Ammon, and upon the people of Moab]

The expression **being cut off of corner** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [all of those who cut off the corner of their hair]

The expression **those being cut off of corner** describes people who trimmed the hair at the sides of their heads as part of the worship of their gods. If your readers would not be familiar with this practice, you could use the name of a similar practice that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [those who trim the hair at the sides of their heads]

Here Yahweh is speaking of the descendants of Israel as if they were a **house**, that is, a single household or family. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the people of Israel]

Here Yahweh is speaking of people who stubbornly refuse to obey him as if their hearts were **uncircumcised**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [are stubbornly refusing to obey me]
